turns.replyText:
Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Absolutely, I can break it down simply. When you shop on our site, these are the main choices you’ll see:

Type of rose (how it grows)
Climbing roses: Long, flexible canes that you tie to an arch, fence, or trellis. Great if you want a wall or arch covered in blooms.
Shrub/bush roses (includes many English/David Austin types): Full, bushy plants that make a nice rounded shape. Great for beds and borders.
Hybrid tea roses: Classic “long-stemmed” roses for cutting, usually one big flower per stem. Great if you want bouquets.
Groundcover roses: Low, spreading plants that cover an area. Good for the front of borders or slopes.
Your climate (hardiness zone)
Every rose has a zone range, like “Zones 5-9.”
You can pick your zone at the top of our website so you only see roses that should do well where you live.
Sunlight
Full sun: Needs about 6+ hours of direct sun each day.
Partial shade: Can do fine with around 4+ hours of sun. Most roses are happiest in full sun.
Size
Each rose has a mature height and width listed in feet, not inches.
This tells you if it will stay small and tidy or become a big showpiece.
Color & fragrance
You can filter by color (pink, red, yellow, apricot, etc.).
You can also filter for fragrance if scent is important to you.
How we ship
All our roses are own-root (grown on their own roots, not grafted) in 1-gallon containers with soil, grown at our nurseries in Oregon.
They arrive defoliated (without leaves) so they travel safely, then leaf out once planted and settled.

turns.replyText:
How do I use it properly the very first time?

Great question – using it right at planting sets your rose up really well.

I’ll walk you through how to use the Get Growing Bundle the first time. The steps are slightly different depending on whether you’re planting in the ground or in a pot.

If you’re planting in the ground

Dig your planting hole first, then:

Cow manure
Put about 3 inches of your regular garden soil in the bottom of the hole.
Mix some cow manure into the soil you removed and use that mix to backfill around the rose.
Bone meal
Mix about 1 cup of bone meal into that backfill soil mixture before you fill the hole.
Mint compost
After planting, spread the mint compost on top of the soil around the base of the rose (this is called a “top dressing”).
Keep it a little bit away from the stem.
Founders fish fertilizer
Mix 4 oz of fish fertilizer in 1 gallon of water.
Water the rose with this mix right after planting.
After that, you can repeat every 4–6 weeks during the growing season.
If you’re planting in a container
Cow manure
Mix some cow manure into your potting soil before you plant.
Fill the pot with this mix and plant the rose.
Bone meal
Mix about 1 cup of bone meal into that potting soil mix before planting.
Mint compost
After planting, spread a thin layer of mint compost on top of the soil around the base of the rose.
Founders fish fertilizer
Mix 4 oz of fish fertilizer in 1 gallon of water.
Water the rose with this mix right after planting.
Then use it every 3–4 weeks during the growing season.
